docs.title: What is Robot Framework?
docs.text:
Robot Framework is a generic, open-source automation framework. It is primarily used for:

  • Test Automation: For web, mobile, desktop, and API applications.
  • Robotic Process Automation (RPA): Automating repetitive business processes.

The framework is built on Python and is highly extensible through the use of libraries and human-readable keywords.

docs.title: History and Evolution
docs.text:
Year Milestone 2004 Concept created by Pekka Klarck — goal of a single, cross-platform automation framework 2005 Design published in Pekka Klarck's master's thesis; first version developed at Nokia Networks 2008 Version 2.0 released as open-source software 2015+ Rapid community growth; adoption in enterprise CI/CD pipelines 2020 Robot Framework 3.2 — major variable and keyword improvements 2022 Robot Framework 5.0 — RETURN, TRY/EXCEPT, WHILE loop, inline IF 2023 Robot Framework 6.x — Tags setting replaces Force Tags/Default Tags 2024 Robot Framework 7.0 — Native VAR syntax, JSON result format, dropped Python 3.7 support

Today the project is hosted on GitHub and maintained by the Robot Framework Foundation, supported by a global community of contributors.

docs.title: Core Philosophy
docs.text: Robot Framework is built around three guiding principles.

docs.title: 1. Human-Readable Tests
docs.text:
Test cases should be readable by anyone — developers, testers, and non-technical stakeholders alike. The keyword-driven approach means a test reads like a specification:

*** Test Cases ***
User Can Log In With Valid Credentials
    Open Browser To Login Page
    Submit Credentials    admin    secret
    Dashboard Should Be Visible

docs.title: 2. Technology Agnostic
docs.text: The framework does not care about the technology under test. The same framework runs web UI tests (via SeleniumLibrary or Browser Library), REST API tests (via RequestsLibrary), database tests, desktop GUI tests, and SSH automation — all with the same syntax.

docs.title: 3. Layered Abstraction
docs.text: Low-level technical operations are wrapped in reusable keywords. Test cases call high-level keywords; high-level keywords call lower-level keywords; the lowest level calls library functions. This layering keeps test cases clean and business-focused.

docs.title: Automation Approaches
docs.text: Robot Framework supports three complementary test automation approaches.

docs.title: Keyword-Driven Testing
docs.text:
Test logic is expressed entirely through keywords. The test writer does not need to know the underlying implementation.

*** Test Cases ***
Search For Product
    Open Browser    https://shop.example.com    chrome
    Search For      laptop
    Results Should Contain    laptop

docs.title: Data-Driven Testing
docs.text:
The same test scenario runs repeatedly with different input data using templates.

*** Settings ***
Test Template    Login With Credentials Should Fail

*** Test Cases ***              USERNAME        PASSWORD
Invalid Username                wrong_user      correct_pw
Invalid Password                correct_user    wrong_pw
Both Fields Empty               ${EMPTY}        ${EMPTY}

docs.title: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD)
docs.text:
Robot Framework supports Gherkin-style Given/When/Then naming conventions. No special plugin is required — the words are simply part of the keyword name.

*** Test Cases ***
Successful Login
    Given the login page is open
    When the user submits valid credentials
    Then the dashboard should be displayed

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    %% Define nodes
    TD[("Test Data\n(.robot, .resource)")]
    Core{"Robot Framework Core\n(Parser → Executor → Result Writer)"}
    StdLib["Standard Libraries\n(BuiltIn, OperatingSystem)"]
    ExtLib["External/Custom Libraries\n(SeleniumLibrary, RequestsLibrary)"]
    SUT["System Under Test\n(Web UI, APIs, Databases)"]

    %% Define relationships
    TD -->|Parsed by| Core
    Core -->|Imports & Calls| StdLib
    Core -->|Imports & Calls| ExtLib
    StdLib -.->|Interacts with| SUT
    ExtLib -.->|Interacts with| SUT

    %% Styling
    classDef core fill:#0073b7,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef data fill:#f39c12,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef lib fill:#34495e,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef sut fill:#2ecc71,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;

    class Core core;
    class TD data;
    class StdLib,ExtLib lib;
    class SUT sut;

The core engine reads test data files, resolves keywords from libraries and resource files, executes them in order, and writes output.xml, log.html, and report.html.

docs.title: About Robot Framework
docs.text: Robot Framework distinguishes itself from other automation tools through its design philosophy and technical architecture.

docs.title: 1. Keyword-Driven Automation
docs.text:
Robot Framework uses a keyword-driven approach. Test cases are written using human-readable keywords rather than complex code.

  • Keywords: Conceptually similar to methods in programming languages.
  • Readability: Makes tests easy to write and understand for both developers and non-technical stakeholders.
*** Test Cases ***
Add Item To Shopping Cart
    Open Product Page    shoes
    Select Size          42
    Click Add To Cart
    Cart Should Contain    shoes    quantity=1

Each line in the test body is a keyword call. Keywords hide implementation details so the test reads as a business specification.

docs.title: 2. Platform and Application Independence
docs.text: Because the core framework is implemented in Python, it is independent of the operating system and the application under test. It runs on any environment that supports Python (Windows, macOS, Linux).

docs.title: 3. Extensibility through Libraries
docs.text: The power of Robot Framework can be extended using libraries, which can be written in Python or Java.

docs.title: Library Types
docs.text: Type Description Examples Standard Bundled with the framework, no install needed BuiltIn, OperatingSystem, Collections, String, DateTime External Community-maintained, installed via pip SeleniumLibrary, RequestsLibrary, AppiumLibrary, Browser Custom Written by your team for project-specific logic Any Python class or module

docs.title: Standard Library Highlights
docs.text:
*** Settings ***
Library    Collections
Library    String
Library    DateTime
Library    OperatingSystem

*** Test Cases ***
Standard Library Examples
    # Collections
    ${my_list}=    Create List    apple    banana    cherry
    Append To List    ${my_list}    date
    Length Should Be    ${my_list}    4

    # String
    ${upper}=    Convert To Upper Case    hello world
    Should Be Equal    ${upper}    HELLO WORLD

    # DateTime
    ${now}=    Get Current Date    result_format=%Y-%m-%d
    Log    Today is ${now}

    # OperatingSystem
    File Should Exist    /etc/hosts
    ${content}=    Get File    /etc/hosts

docs.title: External Library Example — SeleniumLibrary
docs.text:
This project uses robotframework-seleniumlibrary (see requirements-rf.txt).

*** Settings ***
Library    SeleniumLibrary

*** Test Cases ***
Web Login Test
    Open Browser    https://example.com/login    chrome
    Maximize Browser Window
    Input Text      id:username    admin
    Input Password  id:password    secret
    Click Button    id:login-btn
    Title Should Be    Dashboard
    [Teardown]    Close Browser

docs.title: External Library Example — RequestsLibrary
docs.text:
*** Settings ***
Library    RequestsLibrary

*** Test Cases ***
GET Users From API
    Create Session    jsonplaceholder    https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com
    ${response}=    GET On Session    jsonplaceholder    /users
    Should Be Equal As Integers    ${response.status_code}    200
    ${users}=    Evaluate    $response.json()
    Length Should Be    ${users}    10

docs.title: Custom Python Library Example
docs.text:
# libraries/DateUtils.py
from datetime import datetime

class DateUtils:
    """Custom library for date-related helpers."""

    def get_formatted_today(self, fmt="%Y-%m-%d"):
        """Returns today's date in the given format."""
        return datetime.now().strftime(fmt)

    def is_weekend(self):
        """Returns True if today is Saturday or Sunday."""
        return datetime.now().weekday() >= 5

Import it in your test suite:

*** Settings ***
Library    ../libraries/DateUtils.py

*** Test Cases ***
Check Today Is Not Weekend
    ${weekend}=    Is Weekend
    Should Not Be True    ${weekend}

docs.title: Robot Framework 6.x Features
docs.text: This project targets Robot Framework 6.x (robotframework>=6.1.1). Key features available:

docs.title: TRY / EXCEPT — Structured Error Handling
docs.text:
*** Test Cases ***
Handle API Failure Gracefully
    TRY
        ${resp}=    GET On Session    my_api    /endpoint
        Should Be Equal As Integers    ${resp.status_code}    200
    EXCEPT    Connection refused*    type=glob
        Log    API is unavailable — skipping test    WARN
    END

docs.title: WHILE Loop
docs.text:
*** Keywords ***
Wait Until Element Disappears
    [Arguments]    ${locator}    ${timeout}=30
    ${end_time}=    Evaluate    time.time() + ${timeout}    modules=time
    WHILE    True    limit=30
        ${visible}=    Run Keyword And Return Status    Element Should Be Visible    ${locator}
        IF    not ${visible}    RETURN
        Sleep    1s
    END

docs.title: Inline IF
docs.text:
*** Keywords ***
Log Environment
    [Arguments]    ${env}
    Log    ${env == 'prod'}    # inline IF can be used in VAR and RETURN
    ${label}=    Set Variable If    '${env}' == 'prod'    PRODUCTION    STAGING
    Log    Running on: ${label}

docs.title: VAR Syntax (RF 7.x preview)
docs.text:
*** Test Cases ***
VAR Example
    VAR    ${greeting}    Hello, World!
    Log    ${greeting}

docs.title: Ecosystem
docs.text:
The framework provides a robust ecosystem including:

  • RIDE: The Robot Framework IDE — a standalone GUI editor for .robot files.
  • Pabot: Parallel executor for Robot Framework tests.
  • RF-Dashboard / Allure: Enhanced reporting plugins.
  • robocop: Static analysis and linting tool for Robot Framework.
  • robotidy: Automatic code formatter for .robot and .resource files.
  • CI/CD Integration: Native support in Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and Azure DevOps via the output.xml result format.

Next: Installation Guide

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text: This guide walks you through the installation of Python and Robot Framework, including the libraries used in this project.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Python
docs.text:
Robot Framework requires Python 3.8 or higher.

  1. Visit python.org/downloads.
  2. Download the latest stable version of Python (3.8 or higher).
  3. Important: During installation, check the box "Add Python to PATH".
  4. (Optional) Choose "Customize installation" to define a specific directory (e.g., C:\Python311).
  5. Verify the installation:
python --version

docs.title: Step 2: Verify pip
docs.text:
pip is Python's package manager and is bundled with Python 3.4+.

pip --version

If pip is missing, reinstall Python and ensure the pip component is selected during setup.

docs.title: Step 3: Create a Virtual Environment (Recommended)
docs.text:
Using a virtual environment isolates project dependencies from your system Python installation.

# Create the virtual environment
python -m venv .venv

# Activate it (Windows PowerShell)
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# Activate it (Windows CMD)
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat

# Activate it (macOS / Linux)
source .venv/bin/activate

Once activated, all pip install commands install packages into the virtual environment only.

To deactivate:

deactivate

docs.title: Latest Version
docs.text: pip install robotframework

docs.title: Specific Version
docs.text: pip install robotframework==6.1.1

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: pip install --upgrade robotframework

docs.title: Step 5: Install Project Libraries
docs.text:
This project uses the following libraries (defined in requirements-rf.txt):

robotframework>=6.1.1
robotframework-seleniumlibrary>=6.1.3
robotframework-requests>=0.9.5
webdriver-manager>=4.0.1

Install them all at once:

pip install -r requirements-rf.txt

docs.title: SeleniumLibrary
docs.text:
SeleniumLibrary provides keywords for controlling web browsers.

pip install robotframework-seleniumlibrary

docs.title: RequestsLibrary
docs.text:
RequestsLibrary provides keywords for HTTP API testing.

pip install robotframework-requests

docs.title: webdriver-manager
docs.text:
webdriver-manager automatically downloads and manages the correct browser driver binary (ChromeDriver, GeckoDriver, etc.).

pip install webdriver-manager

Usage in a robot test with webdriver-manager:

*** Settings ***
Library    SeleniumLibrary
Library    webdriver_manager.chrome    WITH NAME    WDM

*** Test Cases ***
Open Browser With Managed Driver
    ${driver_path}=    WDM.Install    # downloads ChromeDriver if needed
    Open Browser    https://example.com    chrome
    ...    executable_path=${driver_path}

[!NOTE] Modern versions of SeleniumLibrary (6.x) together with Selenium 4.6+ use Selenium Manager built-in, which handles driver downloads automatically without needing webdriver-manager explicitly. You can simply call Open Browser without specifying a driver path.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify Installation
docs.text:
robot --version

Expected output (version numbers will vary):

Robot Framework 6.1.1 (Python 3.11.x on win32)

Verify all libraries installed correctly:

pip show robotframework robotframework-seleniumlibrary robotframework-requests webdriver-manager

docs.title: Step 7: Freeze Dependencies
docs.text:
Once your environment is set up, export the exact versions for reproducible builds:

pip freeze > requirements-lock.txt

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
Command Purpose python -m venv .venv Create virtual environment .venv\Scripts\activate Activate venv (Windows) pip install -r requirements-rf.txt Install all project deps robot --version Verify RF installation pip show robotframework Show installed RF details pip install --upgrade robotframework Upgrade to latest RF

[!NOTE] If you see robot is not recognized as an internal or external command, ensure that your Python Scripts directory is in your system PATH. See Configuration & IDE Setup for instructions.

Next: Configuration & IDE Setup

docs.title: Configuration & IDE Setup
docs.text: After installing Robot Framework, proper environment configuration and a well-equipped IDE are essential for a smooth development workflow.

docs.title: Environment Variables (PATH)
docs.text:
If you did not select "Add Python to PATH" during installation, manually add the following directories to your system's Environment Variables:

  1. Python Installation Directory: e.g., C:\Python311
  2. Scripts Directory: e.g., C:\Python311\Scripts

Adding these ensures that commands like python, pip, and robot can be executed from any terminal window.

docs.title: Windows — Adding to PATH (GUI)
docs.text:
1. Search for "Environment Variables" in the Start menu.
  2. Click "Edit the system environment variables".
  3. Under System Variables, find Path and click Edit.
  4. Add each directory as a new entry.

docs.title: Windows — Adding to PATH (PowerShell, current user)
docs.text:
$pythonPath = "C:\Python311"
$scriptsPath = "C:\Python311\Scripts"
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable(
    "Path",
    "$env:Path;$pythonPath;$scriptsPath",
    "User"
)

docs.title: VS Code Setup
docs.text: Visual Studio Code is highly recommended for Robot Framework development due to its lightweight nature and powerful extensions.

docs.title: 1. Recommended Extensions
docs.text:
Search for and install the following extensions from the VS Code Marketplace:

  • Robot Framework Language Server (by Robocorp): Provides syntax highlighting, code completion, keyword documentation, and navigation.
  • Robot Framework Intellisense: An alternative extension for syntax highlighting and basic intellisense.

docs.title: 2. Language Server Configuration
docs.text:
After installing the Robot Framework Language Server, add the following to your VS Code settings.json to point it at your virtual environment:

{
  "robot.language-server.python": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/Scripts/python.exe",
  "robot.python.executable": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/Scripts/python.exe",
  "robot.pythonpath": ["${workspaceFolder}"]
}

[!NOTE] On macOS/Linux, replace Scripts/python.exe with bin/python.

docs.title: 3. Key Editor Features
docs.text:
• Syntax Highlighting: Keywords, variables, and comments are color-coded automatically.
  • Go to Definition: Ctrl + Click on a keyword to navigate to its definition in a resource file or library.
  • Keyword Completion: The language server parses imported libraries and resource files and offers autocompletion.
  • Hover Documentation: Hover over any keyword to see its documentation and signature.

docs.title: Static Analysis with Robocop
docs.text:
robocop is the official linter for Robot Framework files. It catches style violations, deprecated syntax, and common mistakes before execution.

pip install robotframework-robocop
robocop --include W0301 tests/

Run it on the entire project:

robocop .

docs.title: Auto-Formatting with Robotidy
docs.text:
robotidy automatically formats .robot and .resource files, enforcing consistent spacing and indentation.

pip install robotframework-tidy
robotidy .

Check formatting without applying changes:

robotidy --check .

docs.title: Recommended Project Structure
docs.text:
A well-organized project is easier to maintain. Here is a recommended folder structure for this project:

MyRobotProject/
├── tests/                  # All .robot files (Test Suites)
│   ├── login_tests.robot
│   ├── checkout_tests.robot
│   └── api/
│       └── user_api_tests.robot
├── resources/              # Reusable keywords and variables (.resource files)
│   ├── common.resource
│   ├── login_page.resource
│   └── locators.resource
├── libraries/              # Custom Python keyword libraries
│   └── DateUtils.py
├── data/                   # External test data (CSV, JSON, YAML, Excel)
│   └── users.json
├── results/                # Execution artifacts (logs, reports — auto-created)
├── .venv/                  # Virtual environment (excluded from Git)
├── requirements-rf.txt     # Project library dependencies
├── .gitignore
└── README.md

docs.title: Why this structure?
docs.text:
• tests/: Keeps test logic separate from implementation details.
  • resources/: Encourages code reuse and modularity.
  • libraries/: Contains custom Python keyword libraries.
  • data/: Separates test data from test logic.
  • results/: Keeps the project root clean by grouping execution artifacts.

docs.title: .gitignore for Robot Framework Projects
docs.text:
Add the following to .gitignore to keep your repository clean:

# Virtual environment
.venv/
venv/
env/

# Robot Framework results
results/
output.xml
log.html
report.html

# Python cache
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*.pyo

# IDE files
.vscode/
.idea/
*.iml

docs.title: Running Tests from VS Code
docs.text:
With the Robot Framework Language Server installed, you can run tests directly from VS Code:

  1. Open the Testing panel (beaker icon in the sidebar).
  2. The extension discovers all .robot files automatically.
  3. Click the run or debug button next to any test case.

Alternatively, use the integrated terminal:

robot -d results tests/

Next: Project Structure & File Anatomy

docs.title: Project Structure & File Anatomy
docs.text: Robot Framework projects are typically organized into folders containing test suites, resources, and configuration files.

docs.title: File Extensions
docs.text:
Robot Framework uses two main file types:

  • .robot: Used for test suites. These files contain actual test cases and can be executed directly.
  • .resource: Used for reusable keywords and variables. These files cannot be executed directly but are imported into .robot files.

[!TIP] Using .resource instead of .robot for shared files makes the project structure self-documenting — it is immediately clear that a .resource file is a library of helpers, not something you run.
